scores.why: The original: real glow and scanlines, but still near-monochrome green on black and the page is flat.
Slate desk with a monitor in a sidebar column is calm and grounded, with a lit tube. It reads as a modern dashboard, and the CRT is mostly the one tube.
The thin track and ring line language the owner loves runs across Home, To do and Chat. A serif head, the haloed tube and several quiet companion colours show across the page content.

The scanlined, bloomed MIND is the strongest CRT moment in the field and the editorial index is a real change. The condensed headings are loud, and the page is black and green with little grounded material.
The drawing-sheet grid, title blocks and pencil rules change the whole page. The scalloped chat bubbles and many pencil colours are busy, and the grid dilutes the glow.

Glowing rails with NOW lamps lead the eye through every section, which is the Signal Box lineage the owner wants echoed. Teal-black materials, a bezelled tube with a grid floor and amber and violet marks are used sparingly.
A calm Swiss page with serif headings and warm grey ink is well typeset and the colour is grounded. The phosphor survives only in the tube and the key, so the CRT soul is thin.
An early slate-and-tube design with a mimic track. It is pleasant and clean, but it is plainer than its descendants.
A lit status line under the question and tighter rows with tabular facts are real refinements. The page looks almost the same as its parent.
The end squares and the press afterglow are nice details. The spend dial is empty in the demo, and at card size the page is nearly the parent.
Track Diagram with banded rows and a 2px coloured cap on each section head gives structure across the content. The Status dial tube is a good instrument, but the demo's empty needle hides it.
Raised keyed filters with lit radio lamps replace selects on Ideas and fit the keypad feel. The typed question and the large count figures are tasteful typesetting on the track page.
The same Lit Index with a dial and section caps. It is the same loud index, and the changes sit on pages the cards barely show.
Heavy rules closed by coloured end blocks and hatched kind swatches add visible structure across the Home index and the Ideas rows. The result is busier, and the hatching is a little fussy.
The huge two-line question over the box is a bold head, and the lit NOW tick on the rail is a good signal. The deeper teal with cream ink is a tasteful ground.
A keypad of filters and an amber bar for late rows are fine and small. The pale blue-grey chosen key is a big light patch, and the rest is the Blueprint again.

Cream ink on teal-black with true small caps and a larger typed count on a heavier rule gives clear typographic and colour variation. It keeps the Grid Console rails and glow, and it is easy on the eyes.

Grid Console rails, a serif heading with a mono label and a thick amber bar for late rows. The chat hung on a rail from Vera's mark and the single Vera card on Home give a quieter, more typeset page that stays a lit CRT.
A title-block foot with a pilot lamp and shorter rows. The change is light, and the date chip moved right scans worse.
The hung chat rail and the haloed mark are lovely and bring the original light back to Swiss Thread. The rest of the page stays plain, and the narrow dates wrap.

The Patch Bay is the most inventive and the richest in material, and the cables echo the line art. The walnut rails and brass read as brown, which the owner has rejected, and the page becomes rack hardware where it should be a CRT.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the rail chat, the serif over mono labels and the amber late bar. Remove the box inside a box on the Home card, and take the cream ink and small caps from mut-9 for more colour variation.
Keep the cream ink on teal-black and the small-cap labels. Make the small caps larger so the gain shows at a glance, and keep the cursor on the count modest.
Keep the rails and NOW lamps as the signature line language. Cut the grid floor and the second hatched strip on Home so the page is quieter, and make the two NOW stamps carry the real clock.
Keep the keyed filters and the lit lamps. The tray is much taller, so tighten it, and carry the same keys to the To do and Plans filters.
The huge question works as a head and the NOW tick is a good signal. Soften the caps from a shout to a lede and carry the tick to To do.
Keep the scanlined, bloomed key word as a signature. Moderate the condensed headings and add grounded material so it is not black with green and amber.
Keep the cable and jack idea as thin line art, and swap walnut for a dark grey-green case so it is no longer brown.

judges.notes: The Grid Console family leads for the owner. Its glowing rails and NOW lamps are the Signal Box line art the owner asked to see echoed, and they delimit areas and lead the eye on every page. The teal-black ground, cream ink and sparing amber, violet and cyan are grounded rather than neon, and the bloom stays on the key word, the tube and the lamps. mut-10 adds a more typeset page with serif headings, a rail chat and an amber late bar, and mut-9 adds the best colour and small caps. Track Diagram and its children (mut-3, mut-4) are strong runners-up, with ring-and-track lines and a visibly different Home. The Swiss and desk families are calm and well made but show too little of the CRT beyond the tube. The Blueprint family changes the whole page, but the grid and the many pencil colours get busy. Lit Index has the best CRT bloom and scanlines, and the Patch Bay is the wildest idea, but its walnut is the brown the owner has rejected. Several mutants of Desk Terminal and Lit Index change things that sit mainly on Status, which the cards barely show, so they look nearly identical to their parents. That repeats the owner's complaint.

parts.what: One Vera card holding the greeting, the question, a lit 'Listening' status line and the box, beside a bezelled tube with a grid floor
Coming up as date cards under a NOW lamp on the rail, with a thick amber bar marking a late task
Thread hung on a rail from Vera's mark, times in the margin, a lit ring at the box
Cream chalk ink on teal-black with sage lit, cyan and sparing amber and violet companions
Source Serif headings and figures over small mono labels, with a tracked small-cap option
Scanlined bloom on the key word, with a glow only on the live things: rails, NOW lamps, tube

scores.why: The real tube light (halo, bloom, scanlines, glow dots) is all there, but it is one note of green and glows on things that are not live.
The question is typed on the glass of a full CRT with a block cursor and the spend dial is a lit moving-coil gauge, so the tube is the page's centre while slate stays grounded.
Keeps the monitor, the lit mind and a listening lamp, but the serif folio and cream ink pull the page away from the tube and little extra light is added.
MIND in scanlined, blooming letters at poster size and a beige 1980s monitor bring back the original light strongly, though the cream and mono-label page cools elsewhere.
Blueprint sheet with a bezelled tube, hatch swatches and a dashed outer bezel is distinctive, but the green lives mostly inside the monitor and the sheet is paper-like.
Teal-black console with a lit home tab, glowing mind and a monitor with a perspective floor reads as a lit instrument, though the Status head is empty and cool.
Swiss serif and grey ink are calm and handsome but the light is reduced to the monitor and one bright button, so the phosphor soul is thin.
Everything on Home is typed on the glass in green mono with a lit dial on Status, which is strongly CRT, but the Ideas head is plain and the page has less structure.
Adds a lit lamp and a status line on the glass and a bold banded dial with a reverse-video LIMIT tag, so the machine feels alive and the green stays on live things.

The dial gets a lit sector, a glowing LIMIT flag, a double bezel and a decaying press afterglow, which is true phosphor behaviour, though the sector is empty in the demo and the end mark is a faint pip.
A dial on Status is good soul but it leaves a big empty tube-less void in the head, and the rest is the serif folio with banded rows.
Latched keys with a lit lamp and a walking block cursor are nice small phosphor touches, but the page around them stays the cool serif folio.
Keeps the blooming scanlined MIND and beige monitor and adds a glowing dial and key afterglow, giving the strongest original light plus a figure, though the dial is not visible on the cards.
Same bloom-lit poster question and monitor with hatched kind swatches and a lamp status line, but the stacked end blocks make the heads busier without adding light.
The huge two-line question with a glowing MIND over a teal sheet is a bold phosphor moment and the NOW tick is a nice live idea, though the bloom is soft and the sheet is quiet.
A keyed filter row and a glowing nav rule are small light touches on the Blueprint, so little changes from the parent.
The typed count with a block cursor on a masthead rule is a real tube gesture, while cream small caps are typographic rather than luminous.
A rail thread and serif headings make the page quieter and more typeset, and the glow shrinks to the monitor and a lamp.
A title-block foot with a pilot lamp is a clever light-on-a-rule idea, but at the head it looks nearly the same as the parent and the phosphor is faint.
The original layered halo returns on the mark and the current page and the thread has a lit ring, which is the right instinct, but the halo is too soft to read.
Walnut rails, a screwed bezel monitor and lamp-keys are a committed physical world and the tube still glows, but the wood and graphite compete with the green.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the glass status line and the banded dial with the LIMIT tag. Carry the glow into the page below the tube (the lit key word, section heads) so the page also has some light.
Keep the lit sector, the flag and the press afterglow. Make the end mark a section colour on the grey bands, not a pip, and show the sector with a non-zero demo spend.
Keep the scanlined, blooming MIND and the beige case. Show the dial in the card crops, and soften the poster so it does not glare at full width.
Keep the huge question with a lit MIND and the NOW tick, but give the glow the layered halo from the kit and scanline texture so it reads as tube light, not a plain highlight.
Keep the screwed monitor bezel and lamp-keys. Cut the wood and the decorative cables so the green is the only light on the rack.
Keep the halo on the mark and the current page, but make it the full layered halo so it shows at 100%, and light only what is live.

judges.notes: The strongest phosphor soul is where the glass carries real content: Desk Terminal's typed question, status line with a lamp, and a dial that is a lit instrument, and Lit Index's scanlined, blooming poster question on a beige case. The Desk Terminal line (head-1, mut-1, mut-2) changes the most across the page: the whole Home is a tube and Status is a gauge. Lit Index is the most faithful return of the original light but stays a bit cool outside the monitor. The serif folio, Swiss and Grid lines are calm and well typeset but lose the tube, and the light on them is mostly the monitor and one key. Blueprint and Patch Bay are bold new ideas: mut-7's giant lit question and Patch Bay's physical rack are worth developing so the green is the only light. Several mutations change one control or one rule, which reads as near identical to their parents at this size.

parts.what: Scanlined, blooming poster word (MIND) plus key afterglow on a beige case
Question typed on the glass with block cursor and a lit lamp status line under it
Large count with block cursor standing on a heavy masthead rule
Lit lamp with a mono status line on the glass; NOW as a lit tick on a rail
Banded moving-coil spend dial on a bezelled tube with a reverse-video LIMIT tag

scores.why: Today's page has the true tube light but reads as one green wash with a timid type hierarchy; the yardstick for tasteful but monochrome.
Desk Terminal in slate is competent and grounded, with a lovely lit monitor column, but it is a quiet, familiar dashboard that does not hit the 'look different' test.
Track Diagram's rail and timeline give the lists real character and the serif count is nice, though the page is still a calm card stack.
Lit Index is the memorable one: scanlined poster 'MIND' with true bloom, condensed grotesque headings, numbered index and hairline rules, a clear magazine-meets-monitor identity across every page.
Blueprint with a title-block sheet header, grid coordinates and cream ink is a fresh, coherent drawing-office idea, though busy and a little fussy.
Grid Console has the most halo and light running through it (circuit rails, NOW chips, floor glow), but the glow is spread widely and the page is dense.
Swiss Thread's light serif display, hanging numerals and blue-and-violet date numerals are the most refined typesetting in the field, but the Home is the least phosphor of the lot.
The early Desk Terminal reference is neat and joined-up but plain next to what has been built on it since.
Adds a lit status line and tighter right-aligned rows to the slate terminal; useful refinement, still the same quiet page.
Square end marks and a dial that cannot be seen at $0 mean almost nothing changes on the cards; a subtle idea that fails to show.
Alternate-row banding and section caps lift Track Diagram's lists a little, but Home is unchanged from its parent.
Raised keyed filters with lamps and a typed question with a walking cursor are tactile touches that make the Ideas page feel like a control panel.
Keeps the Lit Index poster whole and adds section caps and a moving-coil dial, but the additions are on Status and cannot be seen on Home.
Lit Index plus heavy ruled ends in section colours, hatched kind swatches and a lamp-lit status line adds colour and structure across Home, Ideas and Chat while keeping the poster glow.
The huge two-line cream caps question with only MIND lit, plus the NOW tick on the rail, is the boldest Blueprint move and brings the pages' content alive, though loud against its quiet parent.
A joined keypad of filters, a glowing current-tab rule and an amber late bar are good small ideas, but they sit on an otherwise unchanged Blueprint.
Cream ink with true small caps and a big typed count on a masthead rule makes Grid Console warmer and better set, but the serif labels add a fifth face.
A single Vera card on Home, a rail-hung chat and thick amber late bars make Grid Console quieter and more typeset, though the card-in-card heaviness shows.
The drawing title-block foot with a pilot lamp on its rule is a charming end to the page, but the rest is the Swiss parent with a few pixels of rounding.
A chat hung on a rail from Vera's mark with margin times, plus the original halo restored on the mark and current page, gives Swiss Thread some of the lost tube effect.

Patch Bay is the only design with a wholly different material world: walnut rails, engraved graphite modules, condensed caps and cables as rules, with the phosphor saved for scope, lamps and Send; distinctive and lovely, if ornament-heavy.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the poster, hatched kind swatches and status lamp; simplify each section to one heavy rule with the end block and drop the extra hairline so the tops are not busy, and keep the page-head and first-panel end blocks from stacking.

Keep the walnut rails, engraved caps and lamp-and-scope phosphor discipline; cut the decorative cables from heads with no action, use screws and jacks only on the largest plates, and make the Settings lamps mean working rather than merely not flagged.
Keep the huge cream caps question and the NOW tick; scale the question down a step so it does not shout, thicken the rail and tick so NOW holds at half size, and carry the tick to To do.
Fine as the base for the Lit Index line; borrow the ruled ends and status line from mut-6 rather than leaving the index bare.
Keep the rail thread with times in the margin and the restored halo; stop the composer covering the last line, and stop the folio halo lighting words that are not live.
The dial and caps are good but invisible where people look; show the dial on Home or give the caps to Home's own sections.
Keep the cream ink and small caps but use a sans small-cap for labels to avoid a fifth face.

judges.notes: The field is crowded with competent dark dashboards, and the owner asked for change across the page content, not corners. Two directions stand apart. The Lit Index line (poster question with scanlined, bloomed MIND, condensed headings, ruled and numbered index) and Patch Bay (walnut and graphite materials) are the only ones where Home looks different from today at a glance, and both still keep the phosphor on the monitor, the key and the key word. mut-6 is the best of the first, since its ruled ends and hatched swatches colour the structure. Blueprint's mut-7 is the best new move among the mutants: a huge question with one lit word and a lit NOW tick are changes the family would see on Home. The Desk Terminal and Track Diagram mutants make changes the cards mostly do not show (a dial at $0, a pressed-state glow). Swiss Thread is the best typeset but the least tube-like, and mut-12 is the one that brings the halo back.

parts.what: Heavy condensed grotesque headings and poster question over small mono labels, with a numbered index
Walnut rails, graphite panels and bone-brass engraving, phosphor kept for lamps and scope
Huge two-line caps question with only the key word lit, straight over the box
Heavy rule closed by a solid section-coloured end block, with hatched kind swatches
Scanlined, bloomed poster question with a lit lamp status line beside a bezelled monitor
Drawing title-block footer (project, motto, drawn, sheet number)

scores.why: Clear and 17:1 contrast with a legible Home, but 45 of 57 targets are under 44px, the bar is a flat green wash, and the composer is a sea of equal-weight glows.
Joined tube-over-box is a sound Home with zero small targets, but the Ready line and ways to start trail below the fold and the page is mostly green-on-green.
Vera card with the question, composer and chips in a clean top-down read and 1/55 small targets, but the next-up monitor wraps its title to three lines and the sticky tab bar crowds it.
Poster question plus full-width SEND key gives the strongest title-then-action sight line and large targets, but the poster eats half a phone screen and sheen-heavy MIND is loud.
Tube holds the question, next up and a week scope, with a clearly separated composer beneath; 0/62 small targets, a legible open select with a check and a tab bar that underlines the current page.
Blueprint's numbered select list, joined composer row and dashed ways-to-start read as one drafting system, with a status readout (4 plans, 3 late) on the glass; denser and 17 small targets.
Grid Console keeps send inline with the question, a calm bezel and clear NEXT UP monitor; the serif Finish setting heading is cut at the fold but hierarchy is sound; 20 small targets.
Serif question over a plain composer is calm and readable and the thread follows, but 41 of 55 targets are under 44px and the green is thin on the page.

Dialled Slate with a one-line lit status (Listening, watching 4 plans) under the question, a better week scope with NOW and tighter tabular rows; the most glanceable Home, 0 small targets, no loss of any task.
Same sound Desk Terminal Home as the parent; the lit-sector dial, end marks and press afterglow live on Status and key presses, so Home itself shows almost no change.
Track Diagram with a dial on Status and banded rows; Home is identical to its parent, title wraps in the monitor, and a tall empty Status head.
Raised keyed filters latching with a lamp are a good control idea on Ideas and To do, but the Ideas tray grows to 280px and Home shows only a smaller typed question.
Lit Index with a Status dial and section caps; the Home read is the poster plus SEND again, and the changes sit on pages the card does not show.
Adds a mono status line, 44px checkboxes and ring offset to Lit Index, which fixes its two real faults (target size and a blank under the poster); heavy rules plus end blocks get busy.
Question set huge in caps over a joined composer is a clear title, then action, then content read, with a NOW tick on the lists' rails; louder, but a first-time user finds Send at once.
Blueprint with a keyed filter row, a glowing rule under the current tab and an amber bar for late rows, each a readable job; the pale filter patch is heavy and late is missing on To do.
Cream ink and true small caps are a fine typographic move, but the send key drops onto its own row below From and the Fifth face adds weight.
Vera card with the greeting, status line and box nested in a border, a lovely rail chat, but a frame inside a frame, send dropped below From, and a face swap few would notice.
Swiss Thread with a title-block foot and shorter fact-right rows; calm and legible, but 41 small targets and the changes land below the fold.
Vera card with the question, status line, halo on the mark and a thread hung on a rail reads as one conversation system; 43 small targets and the card is boxed tightly.
Walnut rails, graphite modules and patch cables are a coherent system with clear lamp states, but 48 of 55 targets are under 44px and the ornament slows a phone read.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the lit status line, banded dial and tight tabular rows; give the right-aligned WHO and FOR columns more gap from the due text and let the status line carry the late count, as Blueprint's glass does.

Keep the huge two-line question and the NOW tick; cap the question at about 2.4rem on a phone so Send stays above the fold, add a clock time to NOW and give To do a today value so the tick shows there too.
Keep the tube-then-composer order, 0 small targets and the open select with a check; the composer sits a long way down, so lift the Send key to the right of the box.
Keep the numbered select list, joined composer row and glass readout; raise the 17 under-44px targets and calm the dashed chips so they read as one family of keys.
The rack, lamps and cables hold as a system on any page, but pull targets to 44px (the toggle and tick are small), keep one cable per page and shorten the walnut bar on the phone.
Keep the rail thread from Vera's mark and the status line in her card; widen the targets to 44px and drop the card's second border.

judges.notes: Weighing the owner's test (changes across the page content, not a corner), the Desk Terminal family wins on use: it has zero small targets, and the question, status and next-up all sit on one lit tube with the composer beneath. Mut-1 improves the content itself (status line, rows, dial) and mut-7 changes the whole Home hierarchy with a huge question and the NOW tick. Pure Status-only grafts (mut-2, 3, 5) and variants that differ only on pages the card does not show score lower. The Swiss Thread line and Patch Bay have many targets under 44px, which hurts a phone at night. Grid Console variants drop the send key under From on a narrow phone, a small cost to the first-time sender.

parts.what: numbered select list with a check, joined composer row and dashed ways-to-start keys
tab bar marking the current page with a short glowing rule
one-line glass status with a lit lamp (Listening, watching 4 plans)
thread hung on a rail from Vera's mark with times in the margin
huge two-line question with only MIND lit, composer straight under it

scores.why: Yardstick: near-monochrome green on black, every page the same flat card grid; ink and brand contrast of 17/15 is the glare the owner objects to, with only a faint halo.

The monitor rail on the left changes the page's whole structure, and the slate keys and banded sections are grounded. But the slate-blue chosen keys are a big grey-blue patch and the Settings rows read as an editor sidebar.

Serif titles with counted figures, a lit track on Status and a NOW marker on To do change the content on every page. Green stays on the live things. The track is a little long and the Plans clock is a gimmick.

The huge condensed titles and numbered index are a bold, different page, and the typesetting is energetic. The ground is a flat neutral black with a lot of white and yellow, so it is stark and loud rather than calm, and Settings reads like a poster.

The blueprint sheet frame, rulers and grid on every page bring heavy ornament and the costume risk. The cream-and-cyan palette is grounded, but the grid wash looks like a theme, and the line weights are fussy.

The glowing dial, the lit rails with end caps and the grid-floor foot restore the tube's light where it belongs, and the cards are well grouped. The dial floats above the title and leaves a dead gap, and the rail lines run long on every page.

The most varied colour of the field (27% green): serif titles with large light numerals and the Settings rules in six hues. It is calm and well typeset, but the glow is almost gone, the giant Status icon looks stray, and the monitor clips at the card edge.
An early reference: the left monitor rail is a good idea, but the white-grey active tab and the plain rows look unfinished next to its descendants.

The dial with its LIMIT tag, the tighter rows with facts flush right, and amber lines on late tasks all add content-level change. It is nearly the parent in a half-size shot, and the rows overlap through pseudo-element tricks.
A near duplicate of head-1: the lit sector is empty at $0 and the end squares are tiny pips. The only real change is the dial bezel, a corner change.

The big glowing dial in the Status head, a count beside each serif title, the track and the steel-tinted alternate bands. Light is spent where the page's one reading lives, and the colour is grounded. The head is tall and the dial is still empty at $0.
The raised keyed filters with lamps give the To do and Plans controls an identity. Otherwise it is the Folio parent, so the Status page and Settings see no change, and the Ideas tray is taller.
The dial on the Lit Index tube is the only strong graft. The 2px caps are barely visible, the index is stark, and the page still looks like the bold poster parent.

The bright green end blocks on every rule look like progress bars or a loading state, and add noise to a poster page that is already loud. The 44px targets are good, but the stacked end blocks on Status look like an error.
The cyan pencil rules and the lit NOW rail do reach the structure, but the 2px rail disappears at normal size. It adds more line weight to a busy blueprint sheet.
The joined keypad is nice, but the pale blue-grey chosen key is a big light patch and the bar underline is a corner change. It looks like the Cream Breath parent.
Cream ink warms the page, but the block cursor next to the count reads as a broken glyph (5, then a box), and a fifth face (serif small caps) is risky. Gains at half size are invisible.
The quieter serif console: amber bars on late rows are a clear job-bearing signal, and the chat rail is a good idea. The serif swap is subtle, so it risks being called near-identical to head-3.
The title-block foot with a pilot lamp is a charming drawing-sheet detail but it is invisible in most views. The rest is the Swiss parent, and the Plans date column is awkward.
A near duplicate of Swiss Thread: the halo on the mark and current page is a corner effect, and the right-aligned facts are tidy. It does not bring the phosphor back to the content.

A wholly different material language (walnut bar, brass engraving, patch cables). It is the boldest idea and grounded, but it is a costume: the cable under every title is ornament, the brown bar risks a muddy wash, and 48 Home targets are under 44px.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the glowing dial in the Status head and the section-colour caps; shorten the head by putting the deck beside the tube, and let the needle show a sample value so the lit sector is visible. The alternating bands should stay steel-tinted, not grey.

Keep the lit rails and the grid-floor foot as the phosphor light, but bring the dial into the title row so there is no dead gap, and stop the rail running full height on pages with no content to hang on it.
Keep the serif title with its counted figure and the lit track with the NOW marker; drop the Plans clock or fold it into the count, and shorten the vertical track on Status.
Keep the tighter rows with flush-right tabular facts and the late-amber mark; replace the overlap trick with real row padding, and lighten the slate-blue chosen key so it is not a big pale patch.

Keep the engraved plates, lamp-keys and the patch matrix month, which are real material ideas; drop the decorative cable under titles that have no action, make walnut a thinner rule and fix the 48 small targets on Home.
Keep the large light numerals and hue-coded rules on Settings; bring a halo back to the mark and the current numeral and shrink the Status icon so the glow lands where the page is live.
Keep the raised keyed filters with a lit lamp and the typed question; apply them to a parent with a Status head that changes too (the dial), so the whole set of pages moves and not only the controls.
Keep the amber bar for late tasks and the hung chat rail; make the serif change more than a face swap, with a clear size step between heading and label, and fold the rail into one Vera card.

judges.notes: The field splits into three groups. Four are near-duplicates of one parent (the Slate monitors, the Blueprint sheets, the Swiss pages, the Lit Index posters), and their mutants graft a corner dial, an end-pip, or a halo on the nav. Those score low on the owner's test (nearly identical, a corner or a few icons). The designs that change the page's content are Track Diagram (a serif title with a count on every page, a lit track, a NOW marker), Grid Console (lit rails, a tube dial, a grid-floor foot) and the Slate monitor rail. They keep the phosphor where attention belongs and ground everything else. The mut-3 dial in Status's head is the best use of tube light seen: one big lit instrument rather than glow over the page. Biggest hazards: the green end-blocks of mut-6 reading as progress bars, the block cursor beside the count in mut-9 looking like a broken glyph, the Patch Bay's walnut costume, and the Blueprint grid as a wash. Swiss Thread is the calmest and the most colourful but has lost most of the tube's light, which the owner has asked to have back.

parts.what: Serif page title with a large counted figure and small unit, deck line under a hairline rule
To do on a vertical track with dated nodes and a lit NOW marker; tight rows with facts flush right
Moving-coil spend dial on a bezelled glowing tube with a LIMIT flag, in the Status head
Hue-coded 2px rules over each Settings entry; section-colour caps over section heads
Lit NOW node on the track with amber dots for late; a thick amber bar for a late row
Raised keyed segmented filters with a lit radio lamp on the chosen key
